facts: Rachel Rudinger is affiliated with Johns Hopkins University.
Aaron Steven White is affiliated with the University of Rochester.
The research focuses on neural models of factuality.
The study aims to improve the factual accuracy of information in natural language processing tasks.
The study introduces two neural models for predicting event factuality.
The models demonstrate notable performance improvements on three datasets: FactBank, UW, and MEANTIME.
The authors expand the "It Happened" section of the Universal Decompositional Semantics dataset.
The extended dataset is the largest event factuality dataset to date.
The event factuality prediction task (EFP) involves labeling event-denoting phrases with their factuality status.
The authors present two neural models that significantly outperform previous systems on four existing datasets.
The extension of the UDS-IH1 dataset is named UDS-IH2.
UDS-IH2 is the largest event factuality dataset to date.
The authors propose using two bidirectional LSTMs with different topologies to model event factuality.
A linear chain structure outperforms a dependency tree structure in modeling event factuality.
The datasets mentioned for event factuality include FactBank, MEANTIME, and UDS-IH2.
The text reviews existing systems for predicting event factuality that use deterministic algorithms and supervised methods.
The UDS-IH2 dataset includes all predicates in EUD1.2.
A total of 32 annotators from Amazon's Mechanical Turk annotated 20,580 predicates.
The inter-annotator agreement score for the HAPPENED question was 0.84.
UDS-IH2 exhibits a more entropic distribution of factuality ratings compared to other datasets.
The text discusses two neural models for predicting factuality.
One model is a stacked bidirectional linear chain LSTM.
The other model is a stacked bidirectional child-sum dependency tree LSTM.
A two-layer regression model uses the hidden state from the final layer of the stacked model at time t as input.
The stacked bidirectional linear LSTM (L-biLSTM) incorporates layers and bidirectional processing.
The T-biLSTM is an extension of the child-sum dependency tree LSTM.
Both L-biLSTM and T-biLSTM are used to predict the factuality of events associated with words.
The H(ybrid)-biLSTM combines the outputs of both L-biLSTM and T-biLSTM for improved predictions.
The study implements L-biLSTM and T-biLSTM models using PyTorch 0.2.0.
The L-biLSTM model utilizes a standard implementation, while the T-biLSTM employs a custom version from decomp.net.
Both models use 300-dimensional GloVe 42B uncased word embeddings without tuning during training.
Evaluation metrics include mean absolute error (MAE) and Pearson correlation (r).
The L-biLSTM consistently outperforms the T-biLSTM.
The hybrid H-biLSTM excels in correlation on the UW dataset.
The addition of lexical features improves performance on UW but declines on other datasets.
UDS-IH2, the largest dataset, shows the least improvement from multi-task training.
The analysis utilizes the UDS-IH2 dataset and gold dependency parses from EUD1.2.
Contexts without modals or negation exhibit the highest average factuality.
The presence of modals, particularly "will," correlates with lower factuality scores.
A manual error analysis of 50 events reveals that grammatical errors in UDS-IH2 significantly challenge model performance.
The study presents two neural models for event factuality prediction: L-biLSTM and T-biLSTM.
The L-biLSTM generally shows better performance than the T-biLSTM.
The authors created UDS-IH2, the largest publicly available factuality dataset.
Multi-task training across three factuality datasets, including UDS-IH2, yields substantial improvements.
One annotator and 4,179 annotations were removed due to low agreement.
The study involved annotators' agreement on the questions HAPPENED and CONFIDENCE.
The document lists options for instantiating the $TIME pattern variable.
Table 10 presents performance metrics (MAE and r) for multiple models across different datasets.
